source.title_on_document: Guided Creativity: AI Intermediation for Enhancing Originality and Quality in Visual Design

supplement.where: Web Appendix to the paper (WA-1 to WA-25), appended to this PDF at PDF pp. 45-69. The print Appendix A-E (printed pp. 35-43, PDF pp. 36-44) is part of the main document, not a supplement.
supplement.holds: Printed outcome regression coefficients, SEs and contrasts: Tables WA-C.1 to WA-C.4 for Study 1 (PDF pp. 62-64, WA-18 to WA-20), and Tables WA-D.2 to WA-D.5 and Figure WA-D.2 for Study 2 (PDF pp. 67-69, WA-23 to WA-25). The Web Appendix also contains pipeline validation, the replication brief and designer balance table. The main-document appendices contain perception-based originality (Appendix C, Figure C.1, p-values only), Study 1 submission-depth checks and balance (Appendix B and Table B.1), and alignment means/SDs (Appendix E, Table E.3). All these materials are in this PDF; unreported details remain identified in open_questions and final.open_items.

paper_design_summary: Professional freelance logo designers hired on freelancer.com were randomized at registration to a two-week healthcare-brand logo contest with no gallery (Blind), 60 rated human-made exemplars (Open), or AI variations of those exemplars (one or four per exemplar); 440 were randomized and 292 who submitted were analyzed (PDF pp. 17-20, Section 4.1, Figure 4 and Table 1). Submitted logos were scored for survey-based click attractiveness, originality relative to leading exemplars, and secondary alignment; submission counts per designer were also compared. A restaurant-brand replication used Open, Blind, and four variations per exemplar, with 208 designers analyzed from 485 registered designers tabulated by assigned condition (PDF p. 29, Section 5 and Table 2).

studies.label: Field experiment 1: Armor Health healthcare logo contest (main study)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Which gallery the designer could view with the contest brief: none (Blind), the 60 rated original exemplars (Open), one AI variation per exemplar shown with the originals' ratings (Variation(1)), or four AI variations per exemplar with the originals' ratings (Variation(4))
assignment.quote: Upon registration, designers were randomized into one of four conditions: (1) Blind, where they observed only the textual creative brief; (2) Open, where they observed the brief and 60 exemplars with quality metrics;
assignment.locator: PDF p. 19 (printed p. 18), Figure 4 notes; also PDF p. 17 (printed p. 16), Section 4.1

arms.name: Variation(1)
arms.description: Brief plus a gallery of one AI-generated variation for each of the 60 exemplars, shown with the original exemplars' click-attractiveness ratings; the paper's focal treatment arm

arms.name: Variation(4)
arms.description: Brief plus a gallery of four AI-generated variations for each of the 60 exemplars, shown with the originals' ratings; included to test whether more variations per exemplar help

arms.name: Open
arms.description: Brief plus a gallery of the 60 original human-made exemplars (from the brand's 2019 private contest) with their quality ratings

arms.name: Blind

participants.exclusions: 440 designers registered and were randomized at registration (PDF p. 19, Figure 4 notes). Registration did not require participation; the 292 designers who submitted at least one logo were analyzed. Registered minus participating designers, derived from Table 1: Open 35 of 105, Variation(1) 34 of 105, Variation(4) 44 of 120, Blind 35 of 110 (148 in total); Table 1 reports participation of 63.3 to 68.2 percent by arm (PDF p. 20). The output analyses are not intention-to-treat. Quality regressions use all 2,199 submissions of the analyzed designers; embedding-originality regressions use the top 50 submissions by quality per condition (N = 200 submissions, consistent with all four arms), from an unstated number of designers (PDF pp. 62-63, Tables WA-C.1 and WA-C.2).
participants.who: Professional freelance logo designers hired on freelancer.com. The text says participating designers had high client ratings and an average of over 25 completed projects (the Table B.1 arm means of completed projects are 20.96 to 26.08).
participants.quote: A total of 440 designers registered for the experiment, with 292 designers submitting at least one logo (Table 1).
participants.locator: PDF p. 20 (printed p. 19), Section 4.1 and Table 1

ai_tool.name_model: Authors' custom pipeline: each exemplar's prompt combines a trigger-word brief summary derived from the creative brief with an open-form JoyCaption caption of the exemplar image. FLUX.1-dev generates variations from that combined prompt after two LoRA fine-tuning stages: a Logo LoRA trained on about 25,000 logo images from past restaurant contests, and an Optimization LoRA trained with a contrastive loss on 50 survey-rated logo pairs (PDF pp. 10-16, Sections 3.1-3.2.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Researchers generated the variations in advance and displayed them in galleries ranked by the original exemplars' ratings, with 5 pages of 12 source exemplars and the assigned number of variations per exemplar. Only assigned designers could open their gallery during the two-week contest; no condition is described in which designers operated the model themselves (PDF pp. 17-18, Section 4.1). The paper does not state whether designers were told that the variations were AI-generated. Appendix A calls gallery logos previously collected without identifying the condition of the example brief (PDF p. 36).

task.description: Create a new logo for Armor Health, a small-business healthcare brand, in a crowdsourcing design contest with a $400 prize. The brief asked for a logo that makes the brand's Facebook ads more engaging and attracts more clicks; designers were told the goal was logos effective at attracting clicks in online display ads. Designers could submit several logos (2,199 submissions in total). Each day the researchers rated 10 randomly sampled new submissions per condition and sent the ratings privately to their authors. (PDF pp. 17-20, Section 4.1 and Table 1; PDF p. 36, Appendix A.)

outcomes.name: Embedding-based originality of high-quality submissions

outcomes.measure_detail: Originality_i = minimum over the 12 leading exemplars on the gallery's first page of (1 - cosine similarity) between CLIP embeddings (CLIP-ViT-bigG-14-laion2B-39B-b160k). Main sample: top 50 submissions by click attractiveness in each condition (N = 200; the Variation(4) arm is in the regression but its coefficient is not printed). Specification (1): submission-level OLS on condition indicators, submission day, and designer controls (reputation, professionalism, hire again, quality, number of jobs, reviews, hourly rate); SEs clustered by designer. Robustness variants: top 100 per condition, top 200 and top 400 across all submissions (Tables WA-C.2, WA-C.4). This is distance to the original exemplars, which the Variation arms never saw, not similarity across participants.

outcomes.name: Perception-based originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Survey participants rated the similarity of submission-exemplar pairs on color palette, composition, and style (7-point Likert scale, 15 participants per pair and dimension, two calibration pairs shown first). Perceived Originality_i = minimum over the leading exemplars of the average of the three dissimilarity scores. Estimated with specification (1). The paper does not state which submissions were rated or how many. Appendix C labels the AI arm Variation; its interpretation as Variation(1) follows the Section 4.3 cross-reference to the focal perception-based results (PDF p. 22, Section 4.3; PDF pp. 37-39, Appendix C), rather than assuming the label has the same meaning in every appendix.

outcomes.name: Alignment of submissions with the leading exemplars (motif, color, composition)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Secondary mechanism measure: maximum alignment of each submission with the 12 original leading exemplars. The composite combines motif Dice overlap and text-embedding similarity, color-set overlap, color-moment and atmospheric-style distances, and scene-graph and Hu-moment distances; ChatGPT 5.2 extracts motifs and colors (PDF pp. 40-42, Appendix E; PDF pp. 51-53, Web Appendix B.2 and Tables WA-B.1/WA-B.2). No codebook measure category exactly fits this composite. automated_score is retained only as an approximate label for a computed alignment index, not a model rating creativity or an LLM judging creativity; the construct remains other. Higher scores mean greater alignment to exemplars, interpreted as transmission of quality-relevant design elements (rho = 0.453, p < 0.001; PDF p. 42). Table E.3 reports means and SDs for all submissions and top 200, 100, and 50 per condition, without a test or sample-size column (PDF p. 44). It calls the AI condition Variation without identifying arm composition. Table E.2 reports shield prevalence of 0.635, 0.581, and 0.381 in Open, Variation, and Blind (PDF p. 43). A rounding check on the binary feature shares supports pooling the two AI arms but does not confirm the table definition. n_units remains null. statistics_available is empty because no allowed category describes means and SDs without confirmed Ns; all printed statistics remain in reported.

eligibility.reason: S1 alone meets all three criteria. Individual designers were randomized at registration to galleries containing AI-generated logo variations, human exemplars, or no exemplars (PDF pp. 17-19, Section 4.1 and Figure 4); researcher-supplied generative-AI images qualify as ideas_supplied under codebook Sections 3 and 6, without requiring participants to operate the model or know the images are AI-generated. Of 440 randomized designers, 292 were analyzed (Table 1, PDF p. 20), exceeding 50 people. Their submitted logos have survey-based quality scores (PDF p. 5, Introduction; PDF p. 24, Section 4.4; PDF p. 62, Table WA-C.1) and embedding-based originality scores (PDF pp. 22-23, Section 4.3). S2 follows the randomized design and analyzes 208 designers (PDF p. 29, Section 5 and Table 2; PDF pp. 67-68, Tables WA-D.2/WA-D.3). Quality covers all analyzed designers in each study; the unstated designer counts for the top-quality originality subsets do not undermine paper eligibility. Attrition, possible cross-contest overlap, uncertain alignment-arm pooling, and the replication quality table-figure discrepancy affect interpretation or extraction, not satisfaction of the three paper-level eligibility criteria.

one_line_finding: In the main logo contest (292 analyzed designers), AI variations increased mean click-attractiveness quality versus Blind (beta_Var - beta_Blind = 0.0665, SE 0.0197) and top-50 submission originality versus human exemplars (beta_Open - beta_Var = -0.0139, SE 0.0053), with no clear quality difference versus human exemplars or originality difference versus Blind, and the restaurant replication (208 analyzed) showed the same direction pattern (PDF pp. 20 and 29, Tables 1-2; PDF p. 64, Tables WA-C.3/WA-C.4; PDF pp. 68-69, Tables WA-D.4/WA-D.5).
open_questions: Resolved for criterion 1: researcher-supplied AI images qualify as ideas_supplied under the codebook; participants need not operate the generator. The paper does not state whether designers knew the variations were AI-generated (PDF pp. 17-18, Section 4.1; PDF p. 36, Appendix A).

Resolved for criterion 3: originality is distance to the 12 leading original exemplars, not similarity across participants, so it is novelty. No across_people outcome on participant submissions is reported (PDF pp. 22-23, Section 4.3); the model-validation dispersion analysis concerns AI gallery images (PDF pp. 56-57, Web Appendix B.3).

How many distinct designers contributed to each top-quality originality subset? Selection is based on another post-treatment outcome. The counts are submissions, not people (PDF p. 63, Table WA-C.2; PDF p. 67, Table WA-D.2); full-sample quality already establishes analyzed people counts for eligibility.

Resolved for extraction: Variation(1) is the focal Study 1 arm with printed contrasts against Blind and Open; retain it as the primary AI arm (PDF p. 18, Section 4.1; PDF p. 64, Tables WA-C.3/WA-C.4). Variation(4) has only the comparison with Variation(1) in Figure 9 (PDF p. 27).

Documented design limitation: analyses include only designers who submitted; participating-designer balance is not balance for all randomized designers, and the output analyses are not intention-to-treat (PDF pp. 20 and 29, Tables 1-2; PDF p. 37, Table B.1; PDF pp. 65-66, Web Appendix D.1). This does not add a failure under the stated eligibility criteria.

Section 5 does not restate Study 2 assignment timing. The randomized counts use registered designers tabulated by condition and the statement that the replication followed Section 4 (PDF p. 29); exact implementation would require author confirmation.

The paper does not identify whether designers entered both contests. Both used the same recruitment process; confirm cross-study overlap before assigning independent sample_ids (PDF p. 29, Section 5).

Specification (1) lists three condition indicators, while Study 1 N = 2,199 and N = 200 are consistent with including all four arms. Variation(4) coefficients are omitted from the tables; the fitted specification and sample membership need confirmation (PDF p. 23, Equation 1; PDF pp. 62-63, Tables WA-C.1/WA-C.2).

Appendix E does not specify which AI arm or arms form Variation. Table E.2 feature-share arithmetic suggests pooled AI arms, but Table E.3 arm composition and all-submission N remain unconfirmed (PDF pp. 43-44, Tables E.2/E.3).

The final quality-rating survey protocol, number of raters and ratings per output are not stated. Footnote 2 describes sampled in-contest feedback; using that protocol for every final outcome rating is an inference (PDF pp. 18-20; PDF pp. 65-66, Web Appendix D.2).

Figure 11B p-values conflict with the usual normal-approximation checks of Table WA-D.5 coefficient/SE pairs. The PDF does not explain the discrepancy; extract the table coefficients/SEs while retaining the separately reported figure p-values (PDF pp. 30 and 69).
Appendix C does not state which submissions received perception-based originality ratings, their N, or their designer count (PDF pp. 37-39).

Fluency is now recorded, but arm means/SDs and numerical test results are missing; Study 2 does not separately report a submission-depth test. Participant-level submission records would settle these extraction gaps (PDF p. 36, Appendix B; PDF pp. 20 and 29, Tables 1-2).

No codebook measure category exactly fits the composite alignment index. automated_score is explicitly approximate and the construct remains other; the measure definition is recorded in full for extraction (PDF pp. 51-53, Web Appendix B.2; PDF p. 44, Table E.3).
notes: PDF page = printed page + 1 in the main text and Appendix A-E; Web Appendix page WA-k = PDF page 44 + k. Main quality and embedding-originality estimates are submission-level regressions with designer-clustered SEs, designer controls and submission day (PDF p. 23, Section 4.3; PDF pp. 62-69, outcome regression tables); the paper prints no participant-level arm SDs for these outcomes. Appendix C is read as the focal Variation(1) analysis because Section 4.3 directs its perception-based results there. Appendix E cannot be assigned to Variation(1) with the same confidence: its Variation label is unspecified. In a derived rounding diagnostic, the binary Variation feature shares in Table E.2 all admit integer counts with a denominator equal to the sum of submissions from both AI arms, whereas the vertical-layout share cannot be a rounded proportion of the full Variation(1) submission count; this supports a pooling hypothesis but does not establish Table E.3 membership. No inferred alignment N is coded. The automated_score label for alignment is approximate because no exact codebook measure fits this composite. Figures 9 and 10 notes swap panel descriptions; panel titles and the text identify A as originality and B as quality (PDF pp. 27-28). Figure 9 bar heights are not estimated numerically in this form. Figure 11B and Table WA-D.5 have an unresolved inferential discrepancy: for example Open versus Blind is 0.0714 (SE 0.0259) in the table but p = 0.017 in the figure; Open versus Variation and Variation versus Blind also differ from the usual normal-approximation checks. The regression table is the extraction source; no derived replacement p-values are recorded (PDF pp. 30 and 69). The text says designers averaged over 25 completed projects, while Table B.1 gives arm means of 24.60, 21.10, 20.96, and 26.08 (PDF pp. 20 and 37). All arms received private feedback on 10 randomly sampled new submissions per condition per day (PDF pp. 18-20). Fluency outcomes S1-O5 and S2-O3 record submission depth among analyzed designers; no arm means or effect sizes were calculated from totals. Not coded as separate outcomes: the non-randomized refinement comparison (Figure 10, PDF p. 28; Appendix D, PDF pp. 39-40), which reports originality Delta 0.017, p < 0.001 and quality Delta 0.295, p < 0.001 without stating the recruited designer count; and pipeline/model validation in Web Appendices A-B, which does not assign creative participants to AI assistance. Outcome IDs retain the existing originality-first order. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the earlier review record; final dispositions supersede its affected coding statements.

open_items.item: Original question 1, assistance definition: resolved by ideas_supplied; a researcher-generated AI gallery satisfies criterion 1 without direct generator use (codebook Sections 3 and 6; PDF pp. 17-19).
Original question 2, originality versus diversity: resolved as novelty scored on outputs; no across_people result is claimed (PDF pp. 22-23). Criterion 3 is met.

Original question 3, distinct designer counts in top-quality originality subsets and selection by quality: participant-linked submission data would identify each subset. Criterion 2 is already met by full-sample scored quality (PDF pp. 62-63 and 67-68).
Original question 4, primary Study 1 AI arm: resolved as the explicitly focal Variation(1) condition; this primary-arm choice does not affect eligibility (PDF p. 18 and Tables WA-C.3/WA-C.4).

Original question 5, post-assignment nonparticipation and participant-only balance: counts and limitations are documented; analyses are not intention-to-treat, but attrition is not an additional exclusion criterion (PDF pp. 20, 29, 37 and 65-66).

Original question 6, exact Study 2 assignment timing: authors could confirm implementation beyond the stated use of the Section 4 design and randomization checks. Random assignment is supported, and Study 1 independently meets criterion 1 (PDF p. 29).

Original question 7, designer overlap across contests: authors should confirm overlap before independent sample_ids or pooled sample totals are assigned. Each study independently exceeds 50 analyzed people (PDF pp. 20 and 29).

Original question 8, three displayed condition terms versus Study 1 sample sizes consistent with four arms: analysis data/code would identify the fitted specification and omitted Variation(4) coefficient. This affects extraction, not randomized design, people counts or output scoring (PDF pp. 23 and 62-63).
AI-provenance disclosure to designers: authors could confirm what participants were told; awareness is not an eligibility requirement for ideas_supplied (PDF pp. 18 and 36).

Appendix E Variation arm composition and all-submission N: authors must identify included arm(s) and counts. Pooling is plausible but unconfirmed; secondary alignment is not needed for eligibility (PDF pp. 43-44).

Final quality-rating survey design and rater counts: authors could supply the outcome protocol distinct from feedback. Survey-scored participant output is explicit, so criterion 3 is met (PDF pp. 5, 18-20 and 65-66).

Replication quality p-values versus coefficient/SE pairs: authors should reconcile Figure 11B and Table WA-D.5 and identify the testing procedure. This affects inference and extraction, not eligibility (PDF pp. 30 and 69).

Perception-based originality sample membership, output N and designer N: participant-linked rating data would settle missing counts. Eligibility is established by other scored outcomes (PDF pp. 37-39).

Fluency arm means/SDs and numerical tests, especially the unreported Study 2 submission-depth comparison: participant-level submission records would permit extraction. Missing statistics do not affect eligibility (PDF pp. 20, 29 and 36).
Alignment measure vocabulary mismatch: computation and approximate label are explicit, with construct other; no further source evidence is required for screening (PDF pp. 51-53 and 44).
